DelphiR

DelphiR is an R package for the statistical analysis of Delphi studies. It imports and validates the expert ratings, computes descriptive statistics by item, round and indicator, assesses consensus and stability, identifies the items to be submitted to a further round, analyses the written comments of the experts, draws publication-quality figures, and generates a complete round report in HTML or Word format and the controlled feedback for the next round.

Installation

The development version can be installed from GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("yuricalleo/DelphiR")

Data format

Ratings are arranged with one row per expert, one column per item and one numeric rating in each cell:

expert round indicator E1 E2 E3
EXP01 1 impact 9 7 5
EXP02 1 impact 6 5 7
EXP03 1 impact 8 6
  • Empty cells denote missing ratings.
  • The expert identifier is required to follow the same expert across rounds.
  • The round and indicator columns are optional. Without them, each table is treated as a single round and a single indicator, and tables can be combined with delphi_bind().
  • Each indicator has its own rating scale, for example from 1 to 10 or from 1 to 100.

delphi_template() creates an empty Excel or CSV file in this format, with instructions and the code needed to import it. Ratings in long format, with one row per rating, are imported with delphi_data_long() or read_delphi(layout = "long"), and survey exports with two header rows (indicators in the first row, item statements in the second) with read_delphi(header_rows = 2). When identifiers do not denote the same expert in every round, as with response numbers of separate questionnaires, the data should be declared with linked = FALSE, so that rounds are compared as independent samples.

Example 

library(DelphiR)

# Empty template to be filled in
delphi_template("my_delphi.xlsx", items = 12)

# Example data: two rounds, two indicators
x <- delphi_data(
  delphi_example,
  expert_col = "expert", round_col = "round", indicator_col = "indicator",
  scale = list(impact = c(1, 10), plausibility = c(1, 100))
)

x                    # overview
summary(x)           # panel and median [IQR] by item and round
delphi_describe(x)   # descriptive statistics
delphi_consensus(x)  # consensus: IQR at most 20% of the rating scale
delphi_stability(x)  # stability between consecutive rounds
delphi_status(x)     # item status and items for the next round

# Figures, returned as ggplot objects
plot(x, type = "distribution", indicator = "impact")
plot(x, type = "trend", indicator = "impact")
plot(x, type = "consensus")
plot(x, type = "map")

# Expert comments, next to the rating of their author
x <- delphi_add_comments(x, delphi_example_comments)
delphi_comments(x)
delphi_themes(x, by = "theme")

# Round report and feedback for the experts, in Word or HTML format
delphi_report(x, "round2_report.docx")
delphi_feedback(x, "feedback_round3.docx")

See vignette("DelphiR") for an introduction to the complete workflow.

Interactive application

run_app() opens an application in the web browser that covers the same workflow without writing code: import of the ratings and comments by choosing the columns of the file, tables, figures, the analysis of the comments, the round report and the feedback for the experts. The application also writes the R code that reproduces the analysis.

# install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib", "DT"))
run_app()

Consensus and stability

By default, an item reaches consensus when its interquartile range (IQR) does not exceed 20% of the rating scale (von der Gracht, 2012). The scale is measured by its number of points, so that the threshold corresponds to an IQR of at most 1 on a five-point scale and at most 2 on a ten-point scale.

Stability between consecutive rounds is assessed with the Wilcoxon test (signed-rank for linked experts, rank-sum otherwise), with a criterion based on Scheibe, Skutsch and Schofer (1975), which considers an item stable when the net change between the rating distributions of two rounds does not exceed 15%, or with both. Consensus and stability are then combined into four categories:

Status Consensus Stable Further round
Consensus yes yes no
Unstable consensus yes no yes
Stable dissent no yes no
Open no no yes

Citation

To cite DelphiR in publications, use citation("DelphiR").

References

Scheibe, M., Skutsch, M. and Schofer, J. (1975). Experiments in Delphi methodology. In H. A. Linstone and M. Turoff (Eds.), The Delphi Method: Techniques and Applications (pp. 262-287). Reading, MA: Addison-Wesley.

von der Gracht, H. A. (2012). Consensus measurement in Delphi studies: Review and implications for future quality assurance. Technological Forecasting and Social Change, 79(8), 1525-1536. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techfore.2012.04.013
